A weeping angel, wings folded tight, face buried in stone hands, kneeling where the frost never fully thaws.
Draped mourner carved from pale limestone, her veil so thin it seems the wind forgot to move it.
A cracked sundial swallowed by ivy, its gnomon snapped, shadow frozen permanently on the wrong hour.
Fountain figure of a woman pouring nothing from an urn, her basin long since silted into stillness.
Moss-eaten cherub with one eye worn smooth, smiling at something the garden has long since buried.
An armless goddess rising from black soil, her marble throat circled by a collar of dead roses.
Stone archway laced with iron thorns, its keystone carved with a face that weeps perpetual dark water.
A tomb set among the roses, its inscription worn to silence, its lid slightly, permanently ajar.
Gothic gazebo of crumbling limestone, its finials snapped to stumps, its floor a mosaic of fallen leaves.
A draped sarcophagus serving as garden throne, its carved occupant visible beneath cloth-thin stone, still waiting.
Cracked baptismal font repurposed for rainwater, a single stone dove perched on its fractured rim, wingless.
A sundial engraved with the single word NEVER, its pedestal sunk crooked into the black garden earth.
Iron-and-glass folly tarnished to blackness, its panes fogged from within by some permanent interior cold.
A stone girl mid-pirouette, her dress caught in carved wind, one foot lifted above the frozen ground forever.
Weeping fountain-face set into a mossy wall, its mouth perpetually open, its tears long reduced to stains.
A broken obelisk, its hieroglyphs replaced by names no longer spoken, wrapped in the arms of dead wisteria.
A robed stone abbot, hands folded, eyes downcast, standing where the chapel burned and left only him.
Armless Venus half-submerged in a silted pool, her marble shoulders draped with the season's first dead leaves.
A gothic lantern-column of carved stone, its iron cage empty, its light replaced by permanent grey shadow.
Twin mourning figures flanking an empty plinth, each turned away from the other across the frozen pathway.
Stone cradle tangled in black-stemmed rose briars, its carved infant-shape worn smooth by a century of rain.
A lichened urn atop a plinth carved with wings, its mouth stuffed with years of unplanted dark earth.
A stone book left open on a pedestal, its carved pages blank, its spine cracked neatly down the centre.
Hooded pilgrim figure, staff broken at his feet, face hidden in carved shadow, never arriving, never leaving.
A stone mirror frame standing alone in the garden, its glass long gone, reflecting only open winter sky.
A weeping angel, arms outstretched, frost-laced wings spread wide, face buried in stone hands, perpetually grieving toward the frozen earth.
A cracked sundial swallowed by black roses, its iron gnomon bent, the hour it marks long ceased to exist.
A draped mourner kneels at garden's heart, her marble veil so fine it seems to breathe in cold November wind.
A moss-eaten cherub, hollow-eyed and grinning, perches atop a crumbling plinth strangled by ivy black as old grief.
An armless goddess tilts her blind face skyward, lichen gilding her throat, her missing hands buried somewhere beneath the roots.
A stone archway choked with dead wisteria, its keystone carved with a face whose mouth is always slightly open.
A fountain figure stands dry-lipped, one hand raised, water long gone, a deep red stain darkening her marble hem.
A tomb rises among the white roses, its lid askew, the carved name on its face worn deliberately smooth.
A gothic gazebo of blackened iron and frost-fogged glass, its floor a mosaic of broken mirror and cold pale bone.
A crouching stone hound, muzzle pressed to the ground, frozen mid-search, ears pinned flat against its skull in eternal alarm.
A stone nun stands facing the wall, hands clasped, her carved habit split down the back by decades of patient frost.
A baptismal font repurposed as a planter, its basin filled with dark soil, the infant-face carved beneath still watching upward.
A headless seraph, wings folded low, stands where the four paths cross, its neck-stump smooth as if deliberately finished that way.
A stone lectern, open book carved mid-page, each word worn to silence, a single crow feather pressed between its leaves.
A draped sarcophagus, small enough for a child, occupies the garden's centre, pink moss softening the lamb carved on its lid.
An obelisk leans three degrees from true, its hieroglyphs filled with silver lichen, casting a shadow that points toward the locked door.
A veiled marble bride stands among bare rose-canes, her bouquet rotted away, both stone hands still curved around nothing.
A stone well, lidded with a rusted iron grate, its bucket chain descending into dark that absorbs all thrown pebbles silently.
A cruciform sundial, each arm pointing a different compass lie, its motto circling the base reading only what has already passed.
A stone boy mid-run, one foot raised, caught by some ancient spell between one step and the next, forever almost gone.
An urn taller than a man, its carved garlands of nightshade and asphodel undulating up toward a lidded, never-opened mouth.
A stone mirror-frame stands freestanding, no glass within it, only the garden behind seen darkened, somehow, through its empty oval.
A kneeling penitent in hooded stone robes faces east, both palms pressed to frozen ground, a posture of unresolved confession.
A cracked celestial globe, continents wrong and seas unnamed, tilts on its iron axis, one hemisphere darker than the other.
A stone throne, high-backed and carved with thorned vines, sits empty at the garden's end, its armrests worn smooth by no one.
A weeping angel, palms pressed to her stone face, knelt where the frost-killed roses refused to bloom.
The draped mourner's marble shoulders bore a century of green moss and silent, accumulated grief.
A cracked sundial told only one hour, shadow frozen on a numeral no one dared name.
The fountain-figure poured nothing; her tilted urn had been empty since the winter of the disappearance.
A moss-eaten cherub grinned from the overgrown path, one wing snapped, both eyes worn to smooth blankness.
The armless goddess presided over the dead garden, her missing hands implied in every reaching, leafless branch.
A stone archway framed nothing but mist, its carved roses blackened, its keystone split by one precise frost.
The tomb among the roses bore a name half-eaten by lichen and a date that had not yet arrived.
An iron-and-glass folly stood at the garden's heart, its panes milky, its door sealed with old wax.
The gothic gazebo listed slightly eastward, its spires needling a grey sky that never quite broke into rain.
A hooded figure on a plinth, featureless beneath the stone cowl, faced the house with dreadful, patient stillness.
The cracked baptismal font sat in the garden's centre, filled now with black rainwater and one drowned glove.
A sarcophagus lid, propped against the yew, was carved with a face disturbingly similar to the eldest daughter.
The broken obelisk wore its own shadow like a wound, listing where the soft earth had finally relented.
A stone girl mid-curtsy, her expression ceremonial and cold, had stood at the path's end for three centuries.
The lichen-bearded Neptune offered his trident to an empty pool, the stone fish at his feet long silenced.
A draped urn on a high pedestal wept water only in rain, grief requiring the sky's permission.
The seated stone abbot, hands folded on his knees, overlooked the garden with cataract-pale, carved, unreadable eyes.
An angel descended mid-flight, frozen above the frozen garden, one hand extended toward the house's dark upper window.
The moss-swallowed grotto shrine held a niche, and in the niche, a stone Madonna whose face had wept away.
A broken column, ivy-strangled, marked the garden's original axis, its capital lying in the grass like a severed crown.
The stone child at the well's edge leaned perpetually forward, hand almost touching a reflection the black water withheld.
A memorial bench of carved white marble bore an inscription worn past reading, facing only the dead kitchen garden.
The gothic finial, fallen from its spire and half-sunk in moss, still pointed upward with singular, unchastened conviction.
An armored effigy lay flat in the garden, hands crossed on a stone sword, open to every indifferent sky.
A weeping angel, wings folded tight, its stone tears carved mid-fall, eternally grieving into frost-blackened roses.
A draped mourner, marble veil clinging to hollow cheekbones, kneeling at the garden's cold, crumbling heart.
A cracked sundial, its gnomon snapped, shadow frozen on the wrong hour, moss swallowing the numerals whole.
A fountain-figure, arms raised to a sky that no longer answers, water long silenced inside her stone throat.
A moss-eaten cherub, one wing sheared away, blind eyes upturned, half-swallowed by ivy and wet black earth.
An armless goddess on a plinth of cracked marble, her missing hands implied in the cold air around her.
A gothic stone archway, strangled by wisteria and rust-brown vines, the garden beyond visible only as grey shadow.
A tomb among the roses, its lid ajar just enough to trouble the mind on quiet mornings.
A stone sarcophagus, lid carved with a sleeping figure whose smile unsettles, roses pressing through every seam.
A draped urn on a cracked pedestal, the carved cloth impossibly fine, ice collecting in every frozen fold.
A mourning woman hewn from black basalt, her face hidden in her hands, shoulders forever braced against nothing.
A stone gazebo, every arch furred with lichen, its latticed roof collapsed inward like a ribcage long abandoned.
A carved stone throne, too large for any mortal, seated amid frost-killed roses and the silence of dusk.
A shattered obelisk lying diagonal across the path, its inscribed name worn to suggestion by a century of rain.
A baptismal font repurposed by the garden, moss-lined, filled with black rainwater and one fallen stone angel-feather.
A stone maiden, mid-dance, dress carved in violent motion, arrested forever by some sculptor's unrecorded, particular grief.
A grotesque stone face set into the garden wall, mouth agape, frozen in an expression between laughter and horror.
A weathered stone cross, arms wrapped in dead roses tied with ribbon that was once, certainly, white.
A stone sundial shaped as a skull, its shadow marking hours no living occupant has stayed to observe.
A crouching stone figure, robes pooling on the plinth, face pressed to its own knees in total surrender.
A stone birdbath carved with entwined serpents, filled now with ice and one perfect, unidentified feather.
A tall stone column, headless, its capital long fallen, lichen spelling something like a name across the break.
A bas-relief panel set into the garden wall, depicting a procession of hooded figures walking toward a door.
A stone lantern, unlit for decades, its carved panels depicting scenes almost too small and too troubling to read.
A life-size stone effigy laid flat among the roses, hands folded, dressed in carved stone garments of another century.
